newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss go crackers over US bid to curb cheese sales.
newsitem.headline: Swiss go crackers over US bid to curb cheese sales.

text.p: Swiss cheese-makers have reacted angrily to a controversial U.S. bid to ban dairy products made with unpasteurised milk as a health risk, expected to be discussed at a U.N. food safety standards body on Wednesday.

World Health Organisation spokesman Valery Abramov said the United Nations Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is meeting in Geneva this week, was expected to vote on the U.S. proposal before it finishes its current session on Saturday.
"The United States thinks that in terms of public health safety, it is not good to have unpasteurised dairy products for sale. They are proposing an international ban," Abramov said.
The commission sets international food safety standards. Under international trade rules, higher standards must be justified scientifically or risk being challenged as a protectionist measure.
Abramov said statistics showed there were not many cases of foodborne diseases linked to unpasteurised milk products but had no data immediately available.
Members of the U.S. delegation to the meeting of the 150-plus member governments were not immediately available for comment on the proposal, which has angered French and Swiss cheese-makers.
"Europe wants to preserve its cheese from the hygienic imperialism of the United States," said a headline in the French-language Swiss newspaper Le Noveau Quotidien on Tuesday.
"The threat today comes from the United States, which is giving notice of its claim to the pasteurisation of cheese in the planet," the newspaper said.
Diplomats at the Commission, a joint body of WHO and the U.N. Food and Agricultural organisation, said Switzerland and France fiercely opposed the U.S. proposal.

The Swiss Producers Union said Swiss cheese was of highest quality, "a product of craftsmen." Its head, Fernand Cuche, said the art of cheesemaking in Switzerland had been perfected over generations and Swiss cheese was of no risk to human health.
"We demand that the commission continue to allow the circulation of cheese products made from raw milk without hindrance," he told Swiss television.
The Swiss Cheese Union said a potential ban could mainly hit French soft cheese-makers because 70 percent of Swiss production was hard cheese products such as gruyere.
"We're mostly into hard cheese, but France is bigger on soft cheese. Such a proposal could hit the French more than us," said its spokesman, Beat von Burg.
The French are so spoiled for choice from creamy camemberts to roqueforts that late president Charles de Gaulle once observed that a country producing 246 cheeses was ungovernable.
The U.S. share of Swiss cheese exports in 1996 was one sixth of the total foreign sales of 48,000 tonnes, von Burg said.

Some 80 percent of all cheese produced in Switzerland is from unpasteurised milk, but hard cheese must be stored 60 days or more before consumption, thus reducing the risk of foodborne disease, he added.
